title: APES Unit 5: Land and Water Use
description: Modules 24-34 (Friedland & Relyea, 4e). Questions are original, written from the module lecture slides.

questions.q: A coastal town lets every fisher catch as many fish as they like. Each boat keeps catching more, and the fish population crashes. This is an example of:
questions.explain: A shared, limited resource that no one regulates tends to be overused and depleted: the tragedy of the commons.

questions.q: The price of a pair of jeans does not include the cost of the river pollution the factory caused. This unpriced cost is called a(n):
questions.explain: An externality is a cost that results from producing or buying something but is not included in its price.

questions.q: Which U.S. agency manages public land mainly for recreation and conservation, such as Yellowstone and Yosemite?
questions.explain: The National Park Service focuses on recreation and conservation. BLM and USFS allow grazing, mining and timber; FWS focuses on wildlife.

questions.q: Which agency's lands are managed for wildlife conservation, along with hunting and recreation?
questions.explain: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service manages lands for wildlife conservation, hunting and recreation.

questions.q: Which is a likely result of overgrazing on rangeland?
options: Loss of biodiversity and increased erosion
questions.explain: When rangeland is overused, plant cover and biodiversity decline and bare soil erodes.

questions.q: Compared with selective cutting, clear-cutting is:
options: Cheaper per tree harvested but more disruptive and prone to erosion
More expensive and causes less erosion
Harmless to soil because all trees are removed at once
questions.explain: Clear-cutting is economically efficient, but removing nearly all trees disturbs the ecosystem and causes erosion.

questions.q: Why do loggers often avoid selective cutting even though it disturbs less land?
options: It is illegal on federal land
It requires repeated trips and yields less timber at a time, so it earns less
It destroys more habitat per tree than clear-cutting
It only works on tree plantations
questions.explain: Selective cutting removes few trees per visit, so it is less economically beneficial.

questions.q: A land area planted with a single, fast-growing tree species for logging is a:
questions.explain: Tree plantations grow one fast-growing species to be harvested for wood.

questions.q: Which law requires an environmental assessment before federal money or federal land is used for a project?
questions.explain: NEPA mandates an environmental assessment for projects using federal funds or federal land.

questions.q: A developer finds an endangered plant on a parcel. Which law may stop the land from being used commercially?
questions.explain: If an endangered or threatened species lives on the land, the Endangered Species Act can prevent commercial use.

questions.q: During which period were wild plants and animals first domesticated, about 11,000-12,000 years ago?
questions.explain: Domestication of plants and animals marks the First Agricultural Revolution.

questions.q: The Second Agricultural Revolution (1600s-1930s) is best known for:
options: The start of mechanized plowing, planting and harvesting
questions.explain: Mechanization of farming began in the Second Agricultural Revolution.

questions.q: Which of these was NOT an innovation of the Green Revolution?
questions.explain: The Green Revolution added mechanization, fertilizers, irrigation, pesticides and monocropping. Nomadic grazing is a traditional practice.

questions.q: As farms mechanize and grow larger, the average cost per unit of food falls while output rises. This is:
questions.explain: Economies of scale means average costs decrease as output increases.

questions.q: What makes synthetic fertilizer different from organic fertilizer?
options: It is made from plant and animal matter
It is produced commercially using fossil fuels
It adds large amounts of organic matter to soil
questions.explain: Synthetic fertilizers are manufactured commercially using fossil fuels; organic fertilizers come from plant and animal matter.

questions.q: A farmer plants thousands of acres of one crop, year after year. Which problem is MOST likely to increase?
options: Pest outbreaks and the need for pesticides
questions.explain: Monocropping can attract more pests, deplete soil of specific nutrients and increase the need for pesticides and fertilizer.

questions.q: Choosing which plants or animals get to reproduce, rather than letting nature decide, is called:
questions.explain: Artificial selection is humans choosing which organisms reproduce.

questions.q: Which is a commonly cited CONCERN about GMO crops?
options: Higher cost of production for every farmer
questions.explain: Concerns include possible allergies, effects on biodiversity and how GMOs are regulated. Benefits include higher yields and profits.

questions.q: An energy subsidy in agriculture means that:
options: More energy (human and fossil fuel) goes into producing food than the food provides
Crops store more energy than the sun supplies
questions.explain: Mechanized farming puts in more energy from humans and fossil fuels than it gets back as food energy, and shipping food farther increases the subsidy.

questions.q: Farming mainly to feed one's own family is called:
questions.explain: Subsistence farming produces food mostly for the farmer's own family.

questions.q: Which is a NEGATIVE effect of plowing and tilling?
options: Higher rates of wind erosion and more sediment in water
Soil that becomes less compacted over time
questions.explain: Tilling exposes soil, raising wind erosion and sediment in runoff, increasing decomposition (more greenhouse gases), and causing long-term compaction.

questions.q: In slash-and-burn agriculture, burning vegetation helps crops because it:
options: Removes all nutrients from the soil
Releases nutrients stored in the plants into the soil
questions.explain: In nutrient-poor tropical soils, nutrients are held in the vegetation. Burning releases them for a short time.

questions.q: Why do slash-and-burn farmers have to move to new land every few years?
options: The soil becomes depleted of nutrients
Burning is illegal after three years
questions.explain: The nutrients are quickly used up or washed away, so farmers practice shifting agriculture.

questions.q: Which statement about the climate effects of slash-and-burn is correct?
options: It removes CO2 from the atmosphere
Burning releases CO2 and removing forest reduces carbon storage
It has no effect on greenhouse gases
questions.explain: Burning releases CO and CO2, and removing rainforest means less CO2 is taken up and stored.

questions.q: The three major nutrients supplied by modern fertilizers are:
questions.explain: N-P-K: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

questions.q: Fertilizer runs off a farm into a nearby lake. What is the most likely sequence of events?
questions.explain: Extra nutrients fuel algal blooms; when the algae die and decompose, oxygen levels in the water drop.

questions.q: Making synthetic nitrogen fertilizer contributes to climate change because:
options: Fossil fuels used in production release CO2, and nitrogen compounds produce nitrous oxide
questions.explain: Producing the fertilizer releases CO2, and nitrogen compounds in soil produce nitrous oxide, another greenhouse gas.

questions.q: Compared with organic matter, relying only on synthetic fertilizer leaves soil:
options: With no added organic matter, so cation exchange capacity and water retention do not improve
questions.explain: Synthetic fertilizers supply nutrients but not organic matter, so soil CEC and water-holding ability don't increase.

questions.q: Moving to a new plot of land because the soil on the old plot is nutrient-depleted is called:
questions.explain: Shifting agriculture is the pattern of moving on after soil nutrients are exhausted.

questions.q: Worldwide, about 70% of fresh water use goes to:
questions.explain: Agriculture is the largest water use globally, mostly irrigation.

questions.q: An underground layer of permeable rock or sediment that holds groundwater is a(n):
questions.explain: An aquifer stores groundwater in pore spaces, like a sponge.

questions.q: A confined aquifer differs from an unconfined aquifer because it is:
options: Surrounded by impermeable rock or clay
questions.explain: Confined aquifers are bounded by impermeable material. Drilling into one can create an artesian well.

questions.q: When rain percolates down through soil and enters the aquifer, this is called:
questions.explain: Water moving down into the aquifer is groundwater recharge.

questions.q: Which irrigation method loses the LEAST water to evaporation and runoff (about 5%)?
questions.explain: Drip irrigation delivers water slowly right to the roots, losing only about 5%.

questions.q: A farmer applies 1,000 m³ of water using furrow irrigation, which loses about 33%. About how much reaches the crops?
questions.explain: 1,000 x (1 - 0.33) = 670 m³. (Drip irrigation at 5% loss would deliver about 950 m³.)

questions.q: In dry climates, heavy irrigation can cause salinization because:
options: Water evaporates and leaves dissolved salts behind
Salts are added by fertilizer only
Plants release salt through their roots
questions.explain: As irrigation water evaporates, salts build up in the soil and can stunt or kill plants.

questions.q: Over-irrigating so that the A and B horizons stay flooded and plant roots are harmed is called:
questions.explain: Waterlogging floods root zones; it often leads to salinization as well.

questions.q: Many wells pumping from the same aquifer without limits cause a cone of depression. What happens to the water table?
options: It drops around the wells, lowering the water source for all users
questions.explain: A cone of depression is a dip in the water table around heavily pumped wells.

questions.q: A pesticide designed to kill fungi is a:
questions.explain: Fungicides target fungi; rodenticides target rodents; herbicides target weeds.

questions.q: Which pesticide stays in the environment for years to decades?
questions.explain: Persistent pesticides remain for years to decades. Nonpersistent ones break down in weeks to months but may need to be applied more often.

questions.q: Pests that survive a pesticide pass resistance on to offspring, so farmers apply more and stronger chemicals. This cycle is the:
questions.explain: Natural selection favors resistant pests, driving the pesticide treadmill.

questions.q: Herbicide-tolerant GMO crops mainly allow farmers to:
options: Spray herbicide without harming the crop, which saves more crop but does not reduce pesticide use
questions.explain: Herbicide-tolerant crops survive spraying. This protects yield but doesn't cut pesticide use.

questions.q: Why is producing meat less efficient than producing crops for direct human consumption?
options: Animals need more water and land to grow the feed they eat
questions.explain: Raising animals requires land and water to grow their feed, so meat uses more resources per calorie.

questions.q: Large indoor or outdoor facilities that crowd animals together for maximum meat output are called:
questions.explain: CAFOs, or 'factory farms', maximize animals per area.

questions.q: Which is a DRAWBACK of CAFOs?
options: Manure lagoons and heavy antibiotic use
questions.explain: CAFO downsides include confinement, grain feeding, antibiotics, hormones and manure lagoons. Benefits include minimized land costs and feeding efficiency.

questions.q: Roughly what percent of the energy at one trophic level is available to the next?
questions.explain: Only about 10% (10-15% in the lecture) is passed up. That is why eating beef wastes much more of the original crop energy than eating grain directly.

questions.q: Moving herds to seasonally productive feeding grounds, often over long distances, is:
questions.explain: Nomadic grazing follows productive pastures. Free-range grazing keeps animals on grass outdoors most of their lives.

questions.q: Turning productive, low-precipitation land into desert through overgrazing, logging or climate change is called:
questions.explain: Desertification is degradation of arable land into unproductive desert-like land.

questions.q: A fishery collapse is generally defined as a decline of the fish population of:
questions.explain: A collapse means 90% or more of the fish population has declined.

questions.q: Sea turtles and dolphins caught accidentally in nets meant for other fish are:
questions.explain: Bycatch is the unintentional capture of nontarget species.

questions.q: Which policy helps protect fisheries?
options: Maximum catch limits and shorter harvest seasons
questions.explain: Setting maximum catch limits and shortening seasons are sustainable-fishing laws.

questions.q: Which fishing method drags a large net along the ocean floor?
questions.explain: Bottom trawl nets are dragged along the seafloor, capturing large catches (and lots of bycatch).

questions.q: A concentrated accumulation of minerals that is economically worth mining is a(n):
questions.explain: Ores are mineral concentrations that are economically viable to extract.

questions.q: The average concentration of an element in Earth's crust is its:
questions.explain: Crustal abundance is the average concentration of an element in the crust.

questions.q: Removing long strips of surface rock to reach a resource is:
questions.explain: Strip mining removes strips of surface rock or soil to expose the resource.

questions.q: Which mining method uses explosives to remove the top of a mountain?
questions.explain: Mountaintop removal blasts away the summit to reach resources below.

questions.q: Searching river sediments for gold or gemstones is:
questions.explain: Placer mining recovers minerals, metals and stones from river sediments.

questions.q: Waste material left over after the wanted resource is removed from ore is called:
questions.explain: Mine tailings are the unwanted waste returned to the site.

questions.q: Subsurface mining is mining deeper than about:
questions.explain: In the lecture, subsurface mining is more than 100 m (328 ft) below the surface.

questions.q: Why can subsurface mining be economically prohibitive?
options: Safety and insurance concerns make it expensive
questions.explain: Subsurface mining is usually more expensive than surface mining because of safety and insurance costs.

questions.q: Which resources are described as finite reserves, meaning there is a fixed amount in the Earth?
questions.explain: Metals and ores are finite: once the reserves are mined, they are gone on human timescales.

questions.q: A town has 120,000 people living on 250 km². Using the threshold of about 386 people per km², is it an urban area?
questions.explain: 120,000 / 250 = 480 people per km², which is above the 386 per km² threshold.

questions.q: Compared with developed countries, developing countries have:
options: A higher percent urban and fewer of the largest cities
A lower percent urban but most of the world's 20 largest cities
Universal sewage and clean water in all cities
questions.explain: In the lecture, developing nations are about 48% urban versus 75% for developed, yet hold 17 of the 20 largest cities, and some urban areas lack safe water and sewage.

questions.q: Residential areas around a city that are less dense than the city itself are:
questions.explain: Suburbs surround metropolitan centers with lower population density. Exurbs are similar but not connected to a central city.

questions.q: The spread of urban development into rural land, with houses, shops and roads separated by long distances, is:
questions.explain: Urban sprawl is the movement of urbanized areas into rural land.

questions.q: Which is a main CAUSE of urban sprawl?
options: Government policies funding highways and subsidizing suburban mortgages
questions.explain: Cars and highways, affordable suburban living, urban blight and government policies all drive sprawl.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of smart growth?
options: Walkable neighborhoods that mix homes, shops and workplaces
Separating all land uses by highways
questions.explain: Smart growth favors walkable neighborhoods, mixed land use, stakeholder collaboration and preserved open space.

questions.q: Heavy groundwater pumping near a coast lowers the freshwater level, and seawater moves into the aquifer. This is:
questions.explain: Saltwater intrusion happens when a cone of depression near the shore lets salt water flow into freshwater aquifers.

questions.q: Why do parking lots and roads increase flooding?
options: They are impervious, so less water infiltrates and more runs off
questions.explain: Impervious surfaces block infiltration and increase surface runoff.

questions.q: Which strategy would REDUCE urban runoff?
options: Planting trees and replacing pavement with permeable surfaces
Draining rain quickly into storm sewers only
questions.explain: Reducing impervious surfaces, adding trees and capturing rainwater all increase infiltration and evapotranspiration.

questions.q: The area of land and water needed to produce a person's resources and absorb their waste is their:
questions.explain: Ecological footprint measures the area of productive land and water required, usually in hectares.

questions.q: One hectare is equal to about how many acres?
questions.explain: 1 ha = 2.47 acres. (So 10 ha is about 24.7 acres.)

questions.q: A person's ecological footprint is 8 hectares. About how many acres is that?
questions.explain: 8 ha x 2.47 acres/ha = 19.76, or about 19.8 acres.

questions.q: Which best describes the carbon footprint?
options: The amount of land needed to grow food
Total CO2 and other greenhouse gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by a person, country or group
The number of trees needed to build a home
The water used per person each day
questions.explain: The carbon footprint measures greenhouse gas emissions, whereas the ecological footprint measures area.

questions.q: Which is NOT included when calculating an ecological footprint?
questions.explain: Footprints add up land needed for food, water, energy, clothing, housing and transportation.

questions.q: People in developed nations tend to have ecological footprints that are:
options: Larger than those in developing nations
Smaller than those in developing nations
questions.explain: Higher consumption in developed nations means larger footprints per person.

questions.q: True or false: the carbon footprint only counts carbon dioxide, never methane.
questions.explain: CO2 is the main gas counted, but other greenhouse gases such as methane (CH4) can be included.

questions.q: Using a resource without jeopardizing future generations' ability to use it is:
questions.explain: That is the definition of sustainability.

questions.q: Using a renewable resource too fast can turn it into a:
questions.explain: If a renewable resource is used faster than it regenerates, it behaves like a nonrenewable one.

questions.q: Development that balances human well-being today with resource management for future generations is called:
questions.explain: Sustainable development meets today's needs without compromising the future.

questions.q: The maximum sustainable yield (MSY) is the largest harvest that:
options: Can be taken once before collapse
Can be taken indefinitely without depleting the population
questions.explain: MSY is the maximum amount you can take from a resource and keep harvesting it indefinitely.

questions.q: A fish population has a carrying capacity (K) of 10,000. At what population size is harvest generally kept to achieve MSY?
questions.explain: MSY is typically achieved by keeping the population at about half of carrying capacity, here 5,000.

questions.q: Why is MSY hard to set accurately?
options: Birth rates, death rates and carrying capacity are hard to measure, and effects can take years to show
Habitat has no effect on populations
questions.explain: Uncertainty in rates and carrying capacity, delayed feedback, and externalities such as habitat loss and pollution all complicate MSY.

questions.q: Which is a global-scale environmental indicator?
questions.explain: Global indicators include biodiversity, food production, global temperature and CO2, human population and resource depletion.

questions.q: Which factor does the lecture identify as affecting all other environmental indicators the most?
questions.explain: More people create more demand for resources, affecting every other indicator.

questions.q: Rising CO2 from burning fossil fuels is an example of what kind of climate change?
questions.explain: Anthropogenic means caused by humans.

questions.q: Integrated pest management (IPM) aims to:
options: Eliminate all pests using the strongest pesticide
Control pests with several techniques while minimizing pesticide use
questions.explain: IPM combines methods such as crop rotation, intercropping and biocontrol, using pesticides only in small amounts if needed.

questions.q: Planting a different crop on the same field each season to disrupt pest and disease cycles is:
questions.explain: Crop rotation prevents pests from settling in on a single crop.

questions.q: Growing two crops side by side at the same time so one attracts predators of the other's pests is:
questions.explain: Intercropping uses spacing and plant interactions, such as attracting insect predators.

questions.q: Why must scientists study a species before introducing it as a biocontrol?
options: To be sure it eats the target pest and not something else
To make it resistant to pesticides
questions.explain: An introduced species must consume the right pest, or it could create new problems.

questions.q: A farmer plows and plants rows parallel to the slope's elevation lines to slow erosion. This is:
questions.explain: Contour plowing follows the land's topographic contours.

questions.q: Shaping steep hillsides into flat, step-like fields is:
questions.explain: Terracing creates flat steps that slow water and reduce erosion.

questions.q: Planting rows of trees or shrubs at the edge of a field to block wind and prevent soil loss is:
questions.explain: Agroforestry plants vegetation as a windbreak to prevent wind and soil erosion.

questions.q: No-till agriculture helps soil by:
options: Leaving annual crop land unplowed between seasons
questions.explain: Skipping tillage reduces erosion, compaction and the release of stored carbon.

questions.q: Plants grown specifically to be plowed back into the soil at season's end are called:
questions.explain: Green manure adds organic matter and nutrients to the soil when it is plowed under.

questions.q: Rotating livestock among pastures so that no single pasture is overgrazed is:
questions.explain: Rotational grazing gives pastures time to recover.

questions.q: Organic agriculture is defined by NOT using:
questions.explain: Organic agriculture avoids synthetic pesticides and fertilizers and aims to build soil organic matter and biological activity.

questions.q: True or false: sustainable agriculture methods usually require more labor and cost but keep land productive over the long term.
questions.explain: The trade-off is higher short-term labor and cost for long-term productivity.

questions.q: Aquaculture helps meet demand for fish without:
questions.explain: Raising fish allows more food production without taking extra fish from wild fisheries.

questions.q: Which is a criticism of aquaculture?
options: Nonnative fish may escape into the wild
questions.explain: Escapes of nonnative fish, disease spreading through wastewater, and heavy use of feed and medication are common criticisms.

questions.q: Which aquaculture design best prevents fish escapes and disease spreading?
questions.explain: Enclosed above-ground tanks keep fish and waste contained.

questions.q: Replanting trees after a clear-cut, which reduces erosion and begins removing CO2 from the air, is:
questions.explain: Reforestation restocks the forest.

questions.q: Sustainable forestry aims to produce wood while also providing:
options: Clean water, maximum biodiversity and maximum carbon sequestration
The most profit in the shortest time
questions.explain: Sustainable forestry balances timber production with water, biodiversity and carbon storage.

questions.q: Which practice is part of sustainable forestry?
questions.explain: Other sustainable practices: logging with animals instead of heavy machinery, choosing species to maintain richness and evenness, and minimizing wood use.

questions.q: Decades of suppressing every forest fire led to:
options: Less dead biomass on the forest floor
Large quantities of dead biomass, making later fires worse
questions.explain: Suppression allowed dead biomass to accumulate, fueling larger and hotter fires.

questions.q: Fires deliberately set under controlled conditions to prevent worse fires later are called:
questions.explain: Prescribed burns reduce built-up fuel so wildfires are less severe.
